objectives: Reconstruct paleocommunities via Bambach guilds + Sepkoski faunas + isotope paleothermometry.
Trace paleobiogeography from Wegener's drift to dispersal/vicariance + Croizat panbiogeography.
Apply MacArthur-Wilson island biogeography to Quaternary extinctions + de-extinction debates.

slides.title: Paleoecology: communities + diversity through time
slides.body:
**Paleoecology** is the ecology of ancient ecosystems — community structure, niche partitioning, food webs, energy flow, + environmental drivers. Modern paleoecology synthesizes morphology, ichnology, paleohistology, + (especially) geochemistry to recover ecological details from rocks.

**Bambach-Bush-Knoll guilds** — **Richard Bambach** (Smithsonian), **Andrew Bush** (UConn), **Andrew Knoll** (Harvard) — developed a guild-based classification of marine animals using **three orthogonal axes**: (1) **tiering** (vertical position — pelagic / surficial / shallow infaunal / deep infaunal); (2) **motility level** (pelagic / mobile / stationary attached / stationary unattached); (3) **feeding mode** (suspension / surface deposit / mining / grazing / predatory / parasitic). Bambach 1983 originally proposed 6 guilds; Bush + Bambach 2007 + Bush + Bambach + Knoll 2010 expanded to a 6 × 3 × 3 = 54-cell **ecospace cube**. Plot Phanerozoic marine animals into the cube + you see the **explosive expansion of ecospace** through time — particularly across the Cambrian + Ordovician (GOBE — Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event), with novel guilds (mobile carnivores, deep infaunal suspension feeders) filling progressively more of the cube.

This methodology turned biodiversity from a single number (species count) into a multi-axis quantity (functional diversity, ecospace occupation). The 21st-c paleoecological consensus: most major extinctions + radiations are *also* ecospace-restructuring events, not just changes in taxon count.

**Sepkoski's three evolutionary faunas** — **J. John Sepkoski Jr.** (Chicago, 1979 + 1981 + 1984 + 1992) analyzed the Phanerozoic marine genus database + identified **three statistically distinct evolutionary faunas**:
- **Cambrian fauna** — trilobites, inarticulate brachiopods, monoplacophorans, eocrinoids, hyolithids. Dominates Cambrian; declines through Ordovician.
- **Paleozoic fauna** — articulate brachiopods, crinoids, rugose + tabulate corals, stenolaemate bryozoans, cephalopods (esp. nautiloids), ostracodes. Dominates Ordovician through Permian; decimated by end-Permian.
- **Modern fauna** — bivalves, gastropods, echinoids (regular + irregular), malacostracan crustaceans, demosponges, bony fish, sharks, marine mammals. Replaces the Paleozoic fauna across PT boundary; dominates Mesozoic + Cenozoic.

This tripartite division is one of the most robust patterns in macroevolution + the foundation of empirical macroecology. The transitions between faunas align with mass extinctions, confirming that catastrophic events restructure not just diversity but ecosystem composition.

**Paleothermometry**: reconstructing ancient temperatures from rocks is one of paleoecology's great triumphs.
- **δ¹⁸O thermometry** — **Harold Urey** (1893-1981; Chemistry Nobel 1934 for heavy hydrogen + chair of the Manhattan Project) realized in 1947 that the ¹⁸O / ¹⁶O ratio in carbonate fractionates with temperature. Urey + students Epstein + McKinney + Lowenstam developed the carbonate-water thermometer: $T \propto -\delta^{18}O$ — colder water + colder carbonate → more ¹⁸O. The technique requires assumptions about seawater δ¹⁸O (which itself varies with global ice volume), so paleothermometry on Cretaceous foraminifera + dinosaur teeth + Eocene bivalves has uncertainties of ±2-3 °C — but it works.
- **Clumped isotopes** — **John Eiler** (Caltech), Eiler 2007 *Earth + Planetary Science Letters*. Measures the abundance of doubly-substituted ¹³C-¹⁸O bonds in carbonates (Δ47); the abundance depends on temperature *independently of water δ¹⁸O*. This breaks the seawater-composition ambiguity + has revolutionized paleothermometry — applied to Cretaceous seawater, dinosaur body temperatures (Eagle 2011 — sauropods at ~36 °C, theropods at ~32-35 °C), Eocene + Pliocene climates. The method requires precise mass spectrometry + careful sample prep but yields temperatures with ±2 °C precision.

**Other isotopic proxies**: δ¹³C (organic carbon → diet, productivity, atmospheric CO₂ via plant ¹³C fractionation), ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr (provenance + migration), δ¹⁵N (trophic level, food-chain position), δ⁴⁴Ca + δ²⁶Mg + δ⁷Li (more recent additions for biomineralization + climate).

**Diversity through time** — using the **Paleobiology Database (PBDB)** (Alroy + colleagues), the standardized + sampling-corrected diversity curve for Phanerozoic marine animals shows ~250 origination + extinction pulses, the Big Five mass extinctions, + a long Cenozoic rise to ~1500-2500 marine genera by Holocene. Terrestrial diversity (insects, vertebrates) shows similar + arguably steeper rises through the Cretaceous + Cenozoic — partly because of grass + angiosperm + mammalian radiations, partly because of better outcrop preservation.

The paleoecological synthesis lets us reconstruct ancient food webs + community organization + temperature + diet from rocks + isotopes — turning ancient ecosystems into ecological systems we can analyze quantitatively.

slides.title: Paleobiogeography: continental drift to dispersal/vicariance
slides.body:
**Paleobiogeography** combines geography + geology + paleontology to explain the distribution of ancient + modern taxa across Earth's surface. The story is dominated by one of the great revolutions of 20th-c science: **continental drift + plate tectonics**.

**Alfred Wegener** (1880-1930) — German meteorologist + polar explorer. Wegener 1912 (*Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane* — *The Origin of Continents + Oceans*) proposed **continental drift**: continents have moved horizontally through geological time, splitting from a single supercontinent (Pangaea — Greek 'all earth') in the Late Paleozoic + drifting to their present positions. Wegener's evidence: (1) jigsaw-fit of Africa + South America coastlines; (2) matching geology (Hercynian + Caledonian orogens across the Atlantic); (3) matching fossils (*Mesosaurus* in Brazil + southern Africa; *Glossopteris* flora across all Gondwanan continents — South America + Africa + India + Antarctica + Australia); (4) paleoclimatic evidence (glacial striations of similar age in widely separated continents pointing to a coherent Late Paleozoic ice sheet).

Wegener's hypothesis was rejected by most geologists (esp. American + British) for 50 years on the grounds that no mechanism could move continents through oceanic crust. Wegener died in a 1930 Greenland blizzard before vindication.

**Plate tectonics revolution (1950s-1960s)**:
- **Harry Hess** (1962): seafloor spreading at mid-ocean ridges.
- **Frederick Vine** + **Drummond Matthews** (1963 *Nature*): seafloor magnetic stripes — symmetric magnetic anomalies on either side of ridges — proved spreading directly. The Vine-Matthews paper essentially settled the matter.
- **J. Tuzo Wilson** (1965): transform faults.
- **Jason Morgan** + **Dan McKenzie** (1967-1968): mathematical formalization of plate motions.
- By 1970 plate tectonics was the unified theory of solid Earth science. Wegener was vindicated.

**Paleobiogeographic consequences**:
- **Pangaea breakup** (Triassic ~250 Mya through Cretaceous) → modern continental configuration. Created (a) Tethys Ocean (between Africa + Eurasia, closed by ~30 Mya); (b) Atlantic (opened from Jurassic onward); (c) Gondwanan split (South America-Africa Cretaceous, Australia-Antarctica Eocene-Oligocene, India-Africa Cretaceous, India-Asia collision Eocene → Himalayas).
- **Gondwanan biota** — *Glossopteris* + *Mesosaurus* + early dinosaurs + later mammals (marsupials in Australia + South America) show a Gondwanan distribution; Laurasian biota (placentals, conifers, deciduous trees) shows northern continental pattern.
- **Land bridges + corridors** — Bering land bridge (open in Pleistocene low-sea stands), Isthmus of Panama (closed ~3 Mya → Great American Biotic Interchange, GABI), Sunda + Sahul shelves.

**Dispersal vs. vicariance**: two competing explanations for shared taxa on separated continents.
- **Dispersalism** — taxa cross barriers (oceanic dispersal, land bridges) post-separation. Classical biogeography (Wallace, Darwin). Modern proponents: Heads, Brown + Lomolino.
- **Vicariance** — taxa were widespread before continental separation; separation cuts the population in two (vicariant speciation). Classical proponents: **Léon Croizat** (1894-1982; Italian-Venezuelan botanist), Croizat 1958 *Panbiogeography* + Croizat + Nelson + Rosen 1974 'Centers of Origin + Related Concepts'. Croizat introduced **panbiogeography** — overlay multiple species ranges as tracks; nodes where tracks converge = vicariance origins. Heavily criticized initially (Croizat was pre-tectonic plate); vindicated as plate tectonics + cladistic biogeography (Brundin 1966, Hennig, Nelson + Platnick) absorbed his methods.
- Modern view: **both dispersal + vicariance occur**. Bayesian biogeographic methods (RASP, BioGeoBEARS, Yu + Harris) integrate divergence times + plate tectonic reconstructions to estimate dispersal vs. vicariance probabilities for any given clade. New Zealand's biota, southern beeches (*Nothofagus*), ratite birds, marsupials, southern frogs all show signal of both — Gondwanan vicariance + later trans-oceanic dispersal.

**Modern biogeographic regions** (Wallace 1876): Nearctic, Neotropical, Palearctic, Ethiopian (Afrotropical), Oriental, Australian — set by tectonics + climate + history.

slides.title: Island biogeography + Quaternary extinctions + de-extinction
slides.body:
**MacArthur-Wilson Island Biogeography** (1967, *The Theory of Island Biogeography*) — **Robert MacArthur** (1930-1972, Princeton) + **E. O. Wilson** (1929-2021, Harvard). The theory predicts that the equilibrium species richness on an island is set by the balance between **immigration** (decreasing with island isolation + with species richness) + **extinction** (increasing with species richness + decreasing with island area). $S \approx c A^z$ — the **species-area relationship** with $z \approx 0.25$-0.35 for most groups. Larger islands have more species; more isolated islands have fewer.

This simple framework applies to true islands but also to **habitat islands**: mountain tops, lakes, forest fragments, host plants, even **post-extinction refugia**. **MacArthur-Wilson applied to paleobiology**: post-mass-extinction recovery occurs as refugia (effective 'islands' of survivors) re-colonize + repopulate ecospace; isolated landmasses (Madagascar, New Zealand, Australia) preserve relict faunas that elsewhere went extinct.

**Quaternary megafaunal extinctions**: in the Late Pleistocene + Holocene (~50,000 yr - present), most large-bodied terrestrial mammals (>44 kg) went extinct outside Africa:
- **Australia** (~46-40 ka, coincident with human arrival): diprotodons, giant kangaroos, *Genyornis*, *Megalania*, *Thylacoleo*. ~90% of megafauna lost.
- **Eurasia + Beringia** (~40-10 ka): woolly mammoths, woolly rhinos, cave bears, cave lions, *Megaloceros* (Irish elk), Neanderthals + Denisovans.
- **North + South America** (~14-10 ka, coincident with Clovis): mastodons, mammoths, *Smilodon*, dire wolves, giant ground sloths (*Megatherium*, *Glossotherium*, *Eremotherium*), gomphotheres, glyptodonts, native horses + camels, short-faced bears (*Arctodus*). ~80% of large-bodied mammals lost.
- **Madagascar** (~2-1 ka, coincident with Austronesian + later Bantu arrival): elephant birds, giant lemurs, pygmy hippos. ~80% lost.
- **New Zealand** (~750-200 yr ago, with Maori arrival): moas (9 species, *Dinornis* the giant) + Haast's eagle (their predator) + many other birds.

The **'overkill hypothesis'** (Paul Martin 1973): human hunting was the dominant cause, supported by (1) tight correlation with human arrival on every continent; (2) Africa — where humans evolved alongside megafauna — retains most megafaunal diversity; (3) prey naïveté on insular faunas. The **climate-change hypothesis** alone fails to explain the African exception. The **synthesis**: human hunting + climate stress acted synergistically; both contributed, but humans were necessary on most continents (Sandom 2014; Faurby + Svenning 2015; Smith 2018).

**The 6th extinction + paleo-applications**: contemporary biodiversity loss (Pimm + Brooks 1995+; Ceballos 2015; **Anthropocene Working Group** Zalasiewicz) is occurring at ~100-1000× background rates. Paleo-data sets the *background* baseline + the recovery timescale (5-30 Myr from prior mass extinctions). The lesson of paleobiology for conservation: extinctions can be geologically instantaneous, but recovery is geologically prolonged.

**Pleistocene Park + de-extinction**:
- **Sergey Zimov** (Northeast Science Station, Cherskii, Siberia) — Pleistocene Park (1996+): aims to recreate Pleistocene 'mammoth steppe' ecosystems by reintroducing large herbivores (Yakutian horse, bison, musk ox, eventually mammoth-elephant hybrids) to restore grassland-permafrost dynamics + sequester carbon. Theoretical basis: Pleistocene megafauna actively maintained steppe + grasslands; without them, vegetation transitions to less-productive tundra + boreal forest.
- **De-extinction projects**: (1) **Woolly mammoth** — Colossal Biosciences (founded 2021, with George Church + Ben Lamm) — gene-edited Asian elephants with mammoth alleles for cold tolerance; aim for proxy births by 2028. (2) **Thylacine** (Tasmanian tiger) — Colossal + U of Melbourne, Pask lab. (3) **Aurochs** — Tauros Programme back-breeding from cattle. (4) Passenger pigeon, *Christmas Island Pipistrelle*. Critics (Shapiro + Ehrlich + Pyron + others): de-extinction is a distraction from preventing current extinctions; resurrected animals are not ecologically equivalent to ancestors; potential ecosystem disruption.

The paleontological perspective shows that ecosystems re-form + adapt over Myr timescales — but in the human moment, decisions about preservation, restoration, + de-extinction will define the biotic legacy of the next century. Next: **mass extinctions + recoveries** — the great events that shaped Phanerozoic life.

question.question: Apply species-area + island biogeography to a habitat fragment
question.goal: Predict species loss when a habitat patch shrinks.

steps.prompt: MacArthur-Wilson 1967: $S = c A^z$ with z ≈ 0.25. If a forest fragment is reduced from 1000 km² to 100 km², what fraction of species remain?
steps.reveal: $S_{\text{new}}/S_{\text{old}} = (A_{\text{new}}/A_{\text{old}})^z = (0.1)^{0.25} \approx 0.562$. So ~56% of species remain + ~44% go extinct (eventually — at equilibrium). This is the **extinction debt** — extinctions occur over centuries, not instantaneously.

acceptedAnswers: More isolated → lower immigration → lower equilibrium S

steps.reveal: MacArthur-Wilson: equilibrium S is the intersection of immigration (declining with S + with isolation) + extinction (rising with S, falling with area). Greater isolation → lower immigration curve → lower equilibrium. Hence isolated islands (Hawaii, Galápagos) have fewer species than continental shelves of equal area. Same logic applies to habitat fragments: isolated + small = lowest diversity.

steps.prompt: Apply this to the Quaternary megafaunal extinction. When humans arrived in continental Australia ~46 ka, the continent was an effective 'island' for megafauna. Predict the magnitude of loss qualitatively.

acceptedAnswers: Massive loss because prey naïveté + ecological 'island' effect

steps.reveal: Australia's megafauna had evolved without large terrestrial predators since the Miocene + were *prey-naïve*. Human arrival ~46-40 ka produced ~90% extinction within ~5 kyr — comparable to or exceeding the K-Pg extinction in percentage terms, though on a much smaller geographic + temporal scale. The pattern matches MacArthur-Wilson + paleo-naïveté: isolated faunas without predators are highly vulnerable to new ones. The same story plays out in the Americas (~14-10 ka), Madagascar (~2-1 ka), New Zealand (~750-200 yr), + remote oceanic islands.

acceptedAnswers: Reserve size matters; corridors connect fragments; isolated faunas need extra protection

steps.reveal: Conservation implications: (1) **reserve size** — bigger is exponentially better via species-area; (2) **corridors** — connecting fragments increases effective area + immigration; (3) **isolated faunas** (insular endemics, island birds, paleocontinental relicts like lemurs in Madagascar) deserve extra protection; (4) **extinction debt** — patches reduced today will continue losing species for centuries; (5) **resilience timescales** — paleo recovery requires Myr, so ecosystem restoration in human-timescales is essentially impossible at full diversity. The synthesis of MacArthur-Wilson + paleobiology drives modern conservation biology.

question.question: What is the **Bambach-Bush-Knoll ecospace cube** + why is it foundational for marine paleoecology?
options: **Bambach 1983** + **Bush + Bambach 2007** + **Bush + Bambach + Knoll 2010**: a **6 × 3 × 3 = 54-cell** classification of marine animal life modes by **three orthogonal axes**: (1) **tiering** (vertical position: pelagic / surficial / shallow infaunal / deep infaunal); (2) **motility level** (mobile / stationary attached / stationary unattached + faster/slower); (3) **feeding mode** (suspension / surface deposit / mining / grazing / predatory / parasitic). Plot Phanerozoic marine animals into the cube + observe progressive ecospace expansion through time — particularly across the **Cambrian Explosion** + the **Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event (GOBE)**. The framework is foundational because: (1) it shifts macroecology from counting species to characterizing *functional roles*; (2) it makes mass-extinction analysis ecospace-aware — the Permian-Triassic extinction collapsed certain guilds (filter-feeding crinoids, fusulinids) more than others; (3) it lets us ask whether biodiversity 'rises' are also functional rises (yes — the Mesozoic Marine Revolution, Vermeij 1977, expanded predatory + escape guilds); (4) it provides a baseline against which modern human-driven losses can be measured. Combined with **Sepkoski's three evolutionary faunas** (Cambrian + Paleozoic + Modern) — the standard frameworks of Phanerozoic marine macroecology.
question.explanation: Bambach (1983) + Bush + Bambach + Knoll (2010) ecospace cube: 6 tiering × 3 motility × 3 feeding = 54 functional cells for marine animals. Shows ecospace expansion through Phanerozoic — especially Cambrian + Ordovician (GOBE). Foundational for functional macroecology, mass-extinction ecology, + measuring modern losses against deep-time baseline.

slides.workedSolution: Bambach-Bush-Knoll ecospace cube: tiering × motility × feeding mode = 54-cell functional classification. Tracks ecospace expansion through Phanerozoic + GOBE. Companion to Sepkoski's three evolutionary faunas. Foundational for functional macroecology + mass-extinction ecospace analysis.

question.question: Reconstructing a Late Cretaceous paleocommunity
question.prompt: You're studying a Late Cretaceous (~70 Mya) marine community from a chalk platform in modern-day Western Interior Seaway (Wyoming-Kansas). The fauna includes inoceramid bivalves (filter feeders, stationary), ammonites (mobile predators/scavengers), mosasaurs + sharks (pelagic predators), echinoids (deposit + grazing), serpulids (sessile suspension), foraminifera + nannofossils (planktonic). Sketch a paleoecological reconstruction. Address: (1) how you'd assign organisms to Bambach-Bush-Knoll ecospace cells (tiering × motility × feeding); (2) which Sepkoski evolutionary fauna dominates + which is in transition; (3) what δ¹⁸O measurements on foraminifera + bivalve shells would tell you about seawater temperature (Urey thermometry) + how clumped-isotope Δ47 (Eiler) would help control for seawater composition; (4) what δ¹³C + δ¹⁵N tell you about trophic structure; (5) how the community responds to known Late Cretaceous events (sea-level changes, Deccan-related global temperature swings, K-Pg approach); (6) how the **species-area relationship** + MacArthur-Wilson would predict community changes as the seaway transgressed + regressed; (7) which guilds the impending K-Pg extinction will hit hardest + how soon Cenozoic Tethyan biotic interchange will restructure things. Cite Bambach + Bush + Knoll + Sepkoski + Urey + Eiler frameworks.

question.question: MacArthur-Wilson species-area: $S = c A^z$, $z \approx 0.25$. The Amazon rainforest covers ~5.5 × 10⁶ km² + hosts ~50,000 plant species. If deforestation reduces it to 2.0 × 10⁶ km², predict the eventual equilibrium plant species count.
question.hint: $S_{\text{new}} = S_{\text{old}} \times (A_{\text{new}}/A_{\text{old}})^z = 50000 \times (2.0/5.5)^{0.25} = 50000 \times 0.778 \approx 38900 \approx 38000$. ~22% of plant species would be lost at equilibrium — the 'extinction debt' that plays out over decades to centuries. This kind of calculation is central to applying paleobiology + biogeography to modern conservation.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, integrate paleoecology + paleobiogeography to explain how communities + global distributions have changed through deep time.
question.rubric: Mentions: **Paleoecology** uses **Bambach-Bush-Knoll ecospace cube** (tiering × motility × feeding = 54 guilds) + **Sepkoski's three evolutionary faunas** (Cambrian → Paleozoic → Modern) to track functional + taxonomic structure. **Urey** δ¹⁸O paleothermometry + **Eiler** clumped isotopes Δ47 reconstruct ancient temperatures. **Paleobiogeography**: **Wegener 1912** proposed continental drift (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris); vindicated by **Vine + Matthews 1963** seafloor magnetic stripes + the plate tectonics revolution. Pangaea breakup created Gondwanan + Laurasian biotas; **Great American Biotic Interchange** (~3 Mya via Panama). **Dispersal vs. vicariance** — **Croizat 1958** panbiogeography. **MacArthur + Wilson 1967** island biogeography: S = c A^z. Applied to **Quaternary megafaunal extinctions** (Australia ~46 ka, Americas ~14-10 ka, Madagascar ~2-1 ka, New Zealand ~750 yr) — coincident with human arrival, prey naïveté + overkill (Martin). **Zimov's Pleistocene Park** + de-extinction (Colossal mammoth, thylacine) attempt restoration. The 6th extinction (Pimm + Brooks; Zalasiewicz) re-applies these frameworks to today. Concludes: paleoecology + biogeography give the deep-time baseline for conservation.
